note: Beatrice speaks to the souls who stayed behind in the heaven of the stars when Christ and Mary rose out of sight in Canto 23. The feast is from Revelation 19:9: "Blessed are they who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb." The Lamb is Christ, and the food is the sight of God.

Crumbs, like those the dogs eat under the master's table in the Gospel (Matthew 15:27). Dante had used the image before: his unfinished Convivio, the Banquet, offers readers crumbs from the table of wisdom.
God, the source of the truth Dante's mind is thirsting for.

context: She asks the saints to share their knowledge with Dante, then presents him to Saint Peter to be examined.

note: Mechanical clocks driven by gears were a new invention in Dante's lifetime. In a clock the wheels turn at different speeds, one almost still and another racing. The rings of souls do the same.
Dante's word is carole, round dances in which the dancers hold hands and sing. A faster ring means greater joy, and greater joy means a clearer sight of God.

context: The brightest light of the brightest ring. Beatrice identifies him by the keys Christ gave him.

note: Three is the number of the Trinity. Peter circles Dante three times again at the end of the canto.
Dante's Italian uses a painter's image here: our imagination and our speech have colors too crude to paint such folds. A painter needs subtle shades to show the folds of a robe.
Beatrice. All the blessed are brothers and sisters, and the first of the apostles addresses her as an equal.

"I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven", Jesus says to Peter (Matthew 16:19). The popes claimed them as Peter's successors. Beatrice stresses that the keys came down from Heaven and belong to it.

In Matthew 14 Peter steps out of the boat and walks on the water toward Jesus. Then he grows afraid and begins to sink, and Jesus says, "O you of little faith." Beatrice recalls the faith and passes over the doubt.

quote: loves well, hopes well, believes well
context: Dante is examined on each in turn: on faith by Peter here, on hope by James in Canto 25, on love by John in Canto 26.

note: God, in whom the blessed see everything. Peter already knows what Dante believes. The examination is for Dante's sake and for the reader's, a chance to praise the faith aloud.
Faith is what makes a person a citizen of Heaven. No one enters without it, which is why Virgil and the souls of Limbo are shut out.

Dante's word is bachelor, a university student who has passed his first degree. In a medieval disputation the master set a question, the bachelor argued it, and the master alone gave the final ruling. The three examinations follow this pattern.
The first of five questions. Peter asks what faith is, whether Dante has it, where he got it, why he trusts that source, and finally what exactly he believes.
Dante's word is the Latin primipilus, the senior centurion of a Roman legion. Peter is the first officer of Christ's army.

context: Dante quotes the Letter to the Hebrews, which the Middle Ages took to be Paul's. Most modern scholars think someone else wrote it.

quote: set Rome on the right path
note: Peter and Paul both preached in Rome and, by tradition, were both put to death there. The Church honors them together as its founders in the city.

quote: Faith is the substance of what we hope for
note: Hebrews 11:1, almost word for word: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." It was the standard definition in the schools, and Thomas Aquinas builds his account of faith on it.
Dante uses a technical word of the schools, quiditate, "whatness": the answer to the question "what is it?"

quote: among substances and then among evidences
note: Two terms from medieval philosophy. A substance is what stands underneath and holds something up. Evidence, or argument, is the starting point from which reasoning goes on. Peter wants to know whether Dante understands the words or has only memorized them.

quote: Faith takes the nature of substance
note: Dante's answer. The things of Heaven cannot be seen on earth. There they exist for us only as beliefs, and all our hope of Heaven rests on those beliefs. So faith is the foundation, the substance, of hope.

quote: Faith has the nature of evidence
note: The second half. A believer cannot see what he believes, but he reasons from it as from a first premise. So faith does the work of evidence for everything that follows from it.
Hair-splitting argument that only looks sound. Peter's praise is also a jab at the theologians of the schools.

Faith as a coin. Its metal and weight, the definition, have been tested and found good. The next question is whether Dante actually owns it. He says his coin is bright and perfectly round: not worn or clipped, with the stamp plain to see.
Faith is the ground of every other virtue: without it, theologians held, no good act can lead to salvation.

quote: The great outpouring of the Holy Spirit
note: The Bible. Christians hold that the Holy Spirit inspired its writers, and Dante pictures that inspiration as rain poured over its pages. His faith comes from Scripture.
The Old and New Testaments. Dante's Italian calls them the old and new parchments, the skins that books were written on.
Dante's word is syllogism, the formal proof of Aristotle's logic. Scripture persuades him more sharply than any proof of the philosophers.
Miracles. Nature is pictured as a blacksmith, and these are works that never came from her forge. They prove that Scripture has a source above nature.

quote: Only the thing that needs proving
note: Peter spots a circle in the argument. Dante says the miracles prove the Bible is true, but the only witness to the miracles is the Bible.

quote: If the world had converted to Christianity
note: Dante's way out, taken from Saint Augustine's City of God. Suppose there were no miracles. Then a few poor, unlearned men persuaded the whole world of things hard to believe, and that would be a greater miracle than all the rest. Either way there is a miracle, and no one can deny the conversion happened.
Peter and the other apostles had no money, no learning and no power when they set out to preach.

The Church. The apostles planted a vine that bore fruit, and in Dante's day it has become a thornbush. Even in his profession of faith he cannot leave the corruption of the Church unmentioned, and Peter himself takes up the charge in Canto 27.
The Te Deum, the Church's great Latin hymn of thanksgiving, which begins "We praise you, O God." The saints sing it because Dante has passed the first part of the test.
Heaven is pictured as a royal court, with God as emperor and the great saints as his barons. Dante gives the same title to Saint James in Canto 25.
The examination as a climb up a tree, question by question, toward the topmost leaves: the last and hardest question.
The final question has two parts: the content of Dante's faith, and where it came from. His answer is his creed.

On Easter morning Peter and John ran to the tomb of Christ. John, the younger, got there first but waited outside, and Peter went straight in (John 20:3–8). Dante credits the victory to Peter's faith, not his legs.
The opening words of the Creed recited at Mass: Credo in unum Deum.

Aristotle's idea of God as the unmoved mover, taken over by Christian thinkers. God does not push the heavens. They turn out of love and longing for him, while he stays still. The poem's last line says the same: "the love that moves the sun and the other stars".
Arguments from reason, such as those in Aristotle's Physics and Metaphysics. Dante holds that the existence of one God can be proved by philosophy as well as believed from Scripture.

context: Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms: the three parts of the Old Testament as Jesus names them in Luke 24:44. Moses stands for the five books of the Law.

note: The apostles, who wrote the letters of the New Testament. The fiery Spirit is Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came down on them as tongues of flame (Acts 2).

context: The second article of Dante's creed. For the one God he had proofs from reason. For the Trinity he has only the word of the Gospel.

note: Dante's Italian keeps the Latin verbs, sunt and est. God is so truly three and so truly one that grammar allows both the plural and the singular: the Persons are, and God is.
Belief in one God in three Persons is the starting point. All the rest of Dante's faith grows out of it, as a flame grows from a spark.
Peter's blessing, and the sign that Dante has passed. At the start of Canto 25 Dante remembers it as a crowning, and sets it against the poet's crown that Florence has denied him.
